known_vulnerabilities.prevention: Always store secrets (passwords, keys) outside of source code (e.g., environment variables, secret manager) and never keep credentials in plaintext; use strong, adaptive hashing (bcrypt, Argon2) for passwords.
Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. Always use parameterized queries (or an ORM) with placeholders for all dynamic values.

Always escape untrusted data before outputting it into HTML, JavaScript, CSS, or any other interpreter context. Use framework‑provided escaping helpers or a trusted templating engine that auto‑escapes.
Never hardcode cryptographic secrets. Retrieve them from a secure secret store (environment variables, vault, KMS) and rotate them regularly.
Disable debug mode in all non‑development environments. Configure debug flags via environment variables and never hard‑code `debug=True`.
Implement CSRF tokens on all state‑changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH). Validate the token server‑side before processing the request.
Never expose internal exception details, queries, or stack traces to end‑users. Log errors securely and return generic messages to clients.

Do not expose configuration, secrets, or debug information via public endpoints. If such endpoints are required for debugging, guard them behind strict authentication and enable them only in secure development environments.
Always deliver a baseline set of security headers (CSP, X‑Content‑Type‑Options, X‑Frame‑Options, Referrer‑Policy, HSTS when TLS is used) to mitigate common client‑side attacks.

Apply rate limiting to authentication, password reset, and any endpoint susceptible to brute force or abuse. Use a strategy based on IP address, API key, or user identity, and adjust limits to balance security and usability.

Never run a debug‑enabled service on `0.0.0.0` or any externally reachable interface. Bind to localhost or a private network interface in development, and rely on a reverse proxy for external access in production with debug disabled.
Store credentials securely using environment variables or a secrets manager, and use strong password hashing (e.g., bcrypt) for authentication
Always use parameterized queries or prepared statements for database operations
Escape all user input before outputting to HTML, JavaScript, or other contexts
Set secret keys via environment variables with strong, random values; never hardcode in source code
Disable debug mode in production; control via environment variable (e.g., FLASK_DEBUG=False)
Implement CSRF tokens for all state-changing operations (POST, PUT, DELETE) and validate them server-side
Return generic error messages to users; log detailed errors internally for debugging
Restrict access to debug endpoints; never expose secrets, keys, or internal configuration in responses
Implement security headers like CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, and X-XSS-Protection
Implement rate limiting on authentication and other sensitive endpoints to prevent brute-force attacks
Bind development servers to localhost (127.0.0.1) only; use production WSGI servers (e.g., Gunicorn) for deployment
